families.standing: The reeve's house, and the first name on any list
families.reputation: Jocelin keeps the village's tally and is honest about it; Matilda frightens people. Proud, upright, and no use to you in a hard winter.

families.standing: Two houses with the same name and opposite reputations
families.reputation: Winifred's door is open to anyone; Walter's hand is in everyone's pocket. The village forgives the family on her account.

families.standing: A yard everyone needs and nobody enjoys visiting
families.reputation: William will not lower a price, lend a tool or change his mind. Nesta keeps the place honest single-handed.

families.standing: Three houses, the roads between the villages, and more children than money
families.reputation: Reliable, tired and thin on the ground. If something needs moving, a Carter moves it, eventually.

families.standing: One strange house on the rise
families.reputation: Peter measures the stars and asks questions the priest cannot answer; his father is frightened of the dark. Tolerated, quoted, not consulted.

families.standing: Stained hands and the best colour for three villages
families.reputation: Reynold has not changed a method in twenty years and does not intend to. The whole family takes nothing on trust.

families.standing: Downwind, devout, and content with it
families.reputation: William is in the church more than the tanpit and wants nothing from anybody. Harmless, and a little holy.

families.standing: One old woman and a spindle that never stops
families.reputation: Felice Marsh has outworked everyone in the village for fifty years and will not accept help.

families.standing: The loudest house in Wodenshill, and the fullest
families.reputation: Harold promises the moon in a good mood and Hawise quietly settles what he owes. Warm, chaotic, and always owed a favour.

families.standing: A widow, two boys and the only wheel-yard
families.reputation: Winifred feeds other people's children and has not been inside the church in years. Nobody minds.

families.standing: The mill, and the oldest suspicion in any village
families.reputation: Cedric works harder than anyone and takes a little off every measure. Everybody knows. Nobody can prove it.

families.standing: Two houses, one trade, and a quiet war over it
families.reputation: Christina measures to the drop; her brother Gilbert will not be hurried. Between them the village is never dry.

families.standing: A loom, and a wife with plans
families.reputation: Sybil is three schemes ahead of the money and Randal cannot be got to care about any of them.

families.standing: One old man who has never done a day's work
families.reputation: Randal Larkin blesses you, hears everything, repeats it, and lends nothing. The village's news travels through his door.

families.standing: The river, and the best stories on it
families.reputation: Aldric gives away half his catch and lies about the other half. Eleanor is afraid of the water. The boys are on it constantly.

families.standing: A big steady house by the mill stream
families.reputation: Roger writes things down and is asked to witness agreements. Wilmot knows everyone and cares about none of them. Harold is clever and cannot be believed.

families.standing: The kiln at the end of the lane
families.reputation: Drogo acts first and explains later; Bartholomew cannot tell a lie to save his life. An odd pairing that works.

families.standing: Barrels, silence and scripture
families.reputation: Stephen says nothing and endures everything; Jocelin reads and will not be argued out of anything.

families.standing: The newest house in the village
families.reputation: Gunnora and Gilbert married this year. Nothing is known about them yet, which is itself the talk.

families.standing: The hill road and the salt that comes down it
families.reputation: Drogo walks further than men half his age. Agnes says out loud what everyone else is thinking.

ties.note: Warin is Wymond's nephew; the two Carter yards share a horse and argue about it.
Cousins by marriage. Christina minds Wymond's youngest when the roads take him out overnight.
Cousins. Neither of them mentions the third Carter house if they can help it.
Robert is Winifred's nephew, and the only Barrow the priest speaks well of.
Brother and sister, and the two best brewers in the village. They have not agreed on a measure in thirty years.
Joan is Drogo's niece. He got her the place at the Barrow house and has not visited since.
Everyone likes her and nobody likes him, and she has never once said so.
Married this spring. The village is still deciding what to make of them.
Joan is apprenticed into the Barrow household and does more of the work than anyone living there.
The two Winifreds. Between them, no child in Wodenshill goes hungry, and no piece of news goes unrepeated.
Two old women who say exactly what they think and find each other restful.
The one man who asks impossible questions and the one boy who wants to hear them. Peter has not noticed the boy lies about everything else.
Hugh follows Bartholomew about. Between them they have ruined three good stories by telling the truth.
Thirteen and twelve, and on the river when they should be anywhere else.
The two most devout young men in the village, and neither is much fun.
The old man talks and the young man listens, which suits them both.
The reeve keeps the tally; the dyer has never once accepted it. A standing fixture.
Same trade, same name, two doors apart. Each is certain the other waters it.
Seven and seven, and neither will give way about anything at all.
He is attentive and sympathetic; she is waiting to see whether any of it costs him something.
She finds his honesty funny. He has not worked out that she is not laughing at the joke.
Walter owes for a winter of fish. Aldric tells the story of the debt more often than he asks for the money.
Two men who shave a measure, each convinced the other one is worse.
Wilmot holds the gatherings; Matilda has never come to one, and Wilmot has stopped asking loudly.
Harold promised him a cart-load in a good mood and forgot by morning. That was four years ago.
A six-year-old told her she would be judged. Maud has not let it go, which is the funniest thing about it.
She told him to his face that he had never worked a day. He blessed her for it, which made it worse.
